paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Jordan took place near Beverly, New Jersey, on August 6, 1903, when farmers pursuing a Black man accused of robbing a house shot part of his ear off and nearly hanged him from a tree. He confessed to theft with the rope around his neck, was taken down, and was jailed in Beverly. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers from New York to Salt Lake City and across the South, several of which headlined it as a near-lynching.

The man was identified only as a Black man "said to be Frank Jordan, of Media, Pa." According to the dispatch, Samuel Llewellyn saw him coming out of his house, went in, and found that the house had been robbed. Llewellyn gave the alarm and gathered "a number of farmers," who set out to search for the man.

The searchers found Jordan along Rancocas Creek. By their account he would not surrender until a rifle ball "had shot off a piece of one of his ears." The crowd then put a rope around his neck and threw the other end over a tree.

Told to confess, Jordan at first refused. Only when he was "almost lifted from the ground" did he confess to stealing a watch, a ring and some money. The farmers then took the rope from his neck and marched him to Beverly, where he was lodged in jail.

No report of a hearing, indictment or trial for the theft appears in the coverage, and no action against the farmers is reported. The only account of the capture is the farmers' version as relayed in the dispatch; Jordan's own account was not reported.

The Richmond Times Dispatch credited the story to the Associated Press, and on August 7 the same text ran in the Savannah Morning News, the New-York Tribune, the Alexandria Gazette and other dailies. Headlines stressed how close the man had come to death or how the confession was obtained: "New Jersey Farmers Nearly Lynch Negro," "Narrow Escape from Lynching," "Forced to Confess" and "Rope Brings Confession." The Atlanta Constitution, printing it on August 10, headlined it "Jersey Mob Swings Negro Up," and an Iowa paper wrote that the man confessed "as His Feet Are Leaving the Ground."

Condensed versions changed the tone of the story. The Salt Lake Herald called Jordan "a negro thief" and said he had stolen from Llewellyn's store, while the Shepherdstown Register reduced the episode to one line saying the farmers hung him to a tree until he confessed, "which he quickly did." Three South Carolina weeklies, the Batesburg Advocate, the Manning Times and the Marlboro Democrat, ran the dispatch between August 12 and 14 under the title "The New Jersey Way." No report of the episode was found in the Black press.

Most copies place the event on August 6, but one Iowa reprint, datelined August 8, said it happened "yesterday." The full dispatch says Llewellyn's house was robbed, while the condensed Salt Lake Herald version names his store.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Jordan
bases: Farmers who caught a Black man accused of robbery shot part of his ear off, put a rope around his neck over a tree and nearly lifted him from the ground before he confessed and was jailed; headlines called it a near-lynching (A1, A3, A5).

A 'number of farmers' acting without any reported legal authority partly hanged Jordan to force a confession to theft, but removed the rope and turned him over to jail alive, so no one was killed (A1, A3).
Every report is a copy or condensation of one Associated Press dispatch from Beverly (A7), with no local, independent or follow-up account (A1, A3, A6, A13).

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Beverly
accounts.gist: Llewellyn found his house robbed after seeing Jordan leave it; farmers found Jordan along Rancocas Creek, shot off part of his ear when he would not surrender, and hoisted him by a rope until he confessed to stealing a watch, ring and money, then jailed him.

accounts.label: Condensed versions
accounts.gist: Shorter items called Jordan 'a negro thief'; one placed the theft at Llewellyn's store, and another said he confessed 'quickly' once hung to a tree.

framing.detail: Most papers printed the AP text unchanged under headlines stressing the near-lynching or the forced confession: 'Nearly Lynched Negro', 'Narrow Escape from Lynching', 'Forced to Confess', 'Rope Brings Confession'.
The Batesburg Advocate, Manning Times and Marlboro Democrat ran the story under 'The New Jersey Way', locating the violence in a Northern state.
The Shepherdstown Register reduced it to one line treating Jordan as 'a negro thief' who confessed 'quickly'.
